Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Pendleton OR
932 PM PST Wed Nov 4 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...
- Light rain this evening through Thursday morning. 

- Mountain showers return Friday and Sunday morning.

- Breezy weekend winds, primarily late Saturday into Sunday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Current radar and visible satellite imagery shows dry conditions
as clouds begin to develop along the Cascade and Blue Mountains.
This is in response to the high pressure ahead of an incoming
system that is already bringing light showers along the coastal
range. Showers will begin to impact the Cascades after 6PM,
Central Oregon around 9PM, and beginning to spill into the 
Columbia Basin around 11PM. Showers reach the Blue Mountains and
foothills around 3AM and linger into the early morning hours.
Outside of the Cascade and Blue Mountain zones, showers will be
intermittent as rain amounts of up to 0.04" are expected across
lower elevations of the Columbia Basin - most areas will 
receive 0.02" or less. The NBM aligns with these amounts as it 
highlights a 25-45% chance of measurable rainfall (0.01" or 
greater) across lower elevations of the Columbia Basin. Rain 
amounts of 0.08-0.15" are expected across the Cascade and Blue 
Mountains, with higher terrain across the Washington Cascades 
trending on the higher bound of the range and the Oregon 
Cascades and Blue Mountains more toward the lower bounds of the 
range. Snow levels will be hovering around 6000 feet, so the 
only measurable snowfall will occur across the highest terrain 
of the Cascade and Blue Mountains.

An upper level ridge follows closely behind the passing system
Thursday morning, bringing drier conditions and mostly clear
skies for the majority of the day. As a result, high
temperatures will bump up about 5 degrees from Wednesday to near
60 degrees across portions of the Columbia Basin. These
temperatures are about 5 degrees above average for this time of
year, and are expected to stay above normal into next week. The
next system, which is rather weak and well to the north, will 
only clip the Washington Cascades. It does have significantly  
more moisture than tonight's system, but its passing through 
Central British Columbia keeps measurable rainfall confined to 
the Washington Cascades and east slopes. Snow levels will be 
around 8000 feet, so rain is expected. Cle Elum is currently 
along the gradient between a wetting rain (0.10" or greater), 
with higher rain amounts of 0.2-0.3" possible west and at higher
elevations. 

The parent system of this shortwave is forecast to 
pass through Washington Saturday night through Sunday morning. 
The proximity and orientation of this trough passage is expected
to extend rain chances across both the Oregon and Washington 
Cascades, as well as the Blue Mountains. 54% of ensemble 
clusters suggest little, if any, precipitation over lower 
elevations of the Columbia Basin. Timing is trending slightly
slower as well, with 69% of members keeping precipitation 
across the Cascades until early Sunday morning versus moving in
Saturday night. These differences are directly related to the 
strength of the incoming system and the ridge that builds ahead 
of it Friday afternoon/evening. The stronger trough relates to 
a wetter and earlier scenario, with a stronger ridge more 
efficient at weakening and slowing the incoming system.

A secondary concern with the weekend's system will be related to
breezy conditions across Central and Eastern Oregon, primarily
focused on the Grande Ronde Valley. An incoming frontal system,
coupled with high pressure to the southeast and the potential
for cold-pooling in the Grande Ronde Valley will enhance winds
through this area. South winds of 20-30 mph with gusts of 40-50
mph will be possible as the GFS advertises a 4-5mb pressure 
gradient between Baker and Meacham. Currently, the NBM suggests 
a 35-65% chance of wind gusts reaching advisory-level criteria 
of 45 mph or greater. This broad range leads to low confidence 
in advisory-level winds occurring, at least related to current 
guidance. In addition to the large range of NBM probabilities, 
only 46% of ensemble members are suggesting a trend towards 
higher winds for the Grande Ronde. This does seem quite low, but
it is likely the enhancement of cold pooling and a localized 
pressure gradient is not being realized by these longer range 
ensemble members. The arrival of shorter term guidance in the
next 24-48 hours will greatly improve confidence in this event.
75

&&

.AVIATION /06Z TAFS THROUGH 06Z FRIDAY/...Mostly VFR conditions
to prevail through the period. A frontal boundary passage
tonight will bring light rain impacts to sites
DLS/PDT/YKM/ALW/PSC, with precipitation ending before 11Z. CIGs
are expected to remain at or above 3.5kft during and post the
rain band, however there is 20-30% chance that MVFR CIGS may
develop at sites DLS/ALW/YKM tonight through 18Z. Low vsby has
developed at site PSC tonight, so have included in the TAF for
now, with improvement expected by 11Z. CIGs after 17-19Z are
expected to become few-bkn and above 12kft AGL. Winds will be
light, 12kts or less, through the period. Lawhorn/82
